title: Informal fallacies of relevance
note: A fallacy of relevance offers premises that may be true, or emotionally moving, but do not bear on whether the conclusion is true. Attacking the arguer, appealing to pity, force, or popularity, and changing the subject all fit here. The test: even if this premise is true, does it give any reason to believe the conclusion?

read.title: Beside the point
text: Many bad arguments have true premises. Their problem is relevance: the reasons offered, however true or moving, do not bear on whether the conclusion is true. A good test is to grant the premise and ask whether it gives you any reason at all to accept the conclusion.

The most familiar case is the ad hominem, which attacks the arguer instead of the argument. A senator's divorce tells you nothing about whether her budget plan would work. The circumstantial version points to the arguer's interests, and tu quoque points to hypocrisy: a smoker who urges you to quit may be inconsistent, but the advice is still sound. Interests and hypocrisy can be reasons to check an argument carefully; they are not reasons to reject it.

Other fallacies of relevance swap reasons for feelings or pressures: pity, fear, threats, or the comfort of doing what everyone else does. A straw man replaces the opponent's view with a weaker one, and a red herring drags the discussion onto a different topic.

Not every appeal to authority or emotion is fallacious. Trusting a qualified expert inside the expert's field is often reasonable, and emotion is fitting when the facts warrant it. The fallacy lies in letting such appeals substitute for relevant evidence.
